item.title: Google Play Will Block App Updates That Don't Work Properly on Foldables From April (2027)
item.description:
Google will require Android apps on Google Play to work properly on foldable phones. Under new adaptive app quality requirements that take effect in April 2027, apps that fall short will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play and may become harder to find in the store.

Google says owners of premium foldable phones expect their apps to switch smoothly between the folded and unfolded screens. The company counts more than 580 million large-screen Android devices in use today, from foldables and tablets to Amazon's Alexa tablets, Googlebook laptops and Android XR devices like the XREAL Aura.

It recommends that developers build adaptive layouts with modern UI toolkits like Jetpack Compose, so the same app scales from phones to foldables and tablets.

What Android Apps Must Do on Foldables

Apps will need to meet at least Tier 3, called "adaptive ready," of Android's adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables. In practice, that means apps have to:

  • fill the foldable's full display without letterboxing or compatibility modes
  • keep text and playback state when the device is rotated, folded or unfolded
  • support multi window use
  • target API level 37 (Android 17), which removes the developer opt outs for orientation and resizing restrictions on large screens

Tier 2 ("adaptive optimized") and Tier 1 ("adaptive differentiated") offer a better experience on foldables. Google says Play's quality framework will gradually expand to include those tiers across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks and Android XR. Apps that reach them can get store badges, editorial spotlights and enhanced merchandising on Google Play.

Google Play Foldable Requirements Timeline

The changes arrive in stages:

  1. Now: developers can upload foldable screenshots in Play Console, showing both the inner and outer screens.
  2. April 2027: Tier 3 becomes the minimum for apps that publish or update, and listings need 3 foldable screenshots in addition to the 2 standard phone screenshots.
  3. August 2027: separate large screen requirements apply to games, which Google has published as a dedicated set of quality rules for game developers.

Google points developers to the Android CLI and the Android Emulator to capture screenshots that are ready for Play Console, so developers without a foldable device can still meet the screenshot requirement.

Older apps that are not updated stay available to download, but they may have reduced visibility on the store. Screenshots can come from physical devices or the Android Emulator.

For users, the change means fewer stretched, letterboxed or broken apps on the inner screens of foldable phones, at least among apps that are still updated. Google says it is also working on future requirements for tablets, Chromebooks and other large screen devices.

item.title: UK Court Forces Government to Confirm It Ordered Apple to Open iCloud Encryption (2026)
item.description:
The UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The tribunal rejected the Home Office's argument that confirming the notice exists would damage national security.

The Home Office had followed its usual "neither confirm nor deny" policy on the case. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials and media briefings that they concluded the UK government had authorized.

What the Apple Backdoor Ruling Means

A Technical Capability Notice is issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. It forces companies to make technical changes that support the UK government's legal surveillance powers. The ruling confirms only that the notice exists. Its exact demands stay secret for now.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment states.

The judges agreed that disclosing all the material would harm national security, but said not every detail has to stay secret, and that the exact boundaries cannot be set yet.

The case so far:

  • January 2025: the Home Office demands an iCloud backdoor, which becomes public in February 2025
  • February 2025: Apple removes Advanced Data Protection for UK users
  • August 2025: US officials say the UK agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data
  • October 2025: the UK reportedly replaces the original notice with a new order focused on British users
  • July 2026: Apple files a second legal challenge after its first was dismissed
  • first half of 2027: a full hearing is planned

Advanced Data Protection in the UK

Advanced Data Protection extends end to end encryption to more iCloud data, including backups, photos and notes. Only the user's trusted devices hold the keys, so Apple cannot decrypt that data for investigators.

Without it, the data is still encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can hand content over in response to valid legal demands. Some categories stay end to end encrypted either way. The feature is still available in the US.

A government spokesperson defended the powers. "The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public," the spokesperson said, adding that the government "never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data" and that the notice "simply requires that they maintain the ability" to help police.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the notice regime from Liberty, Privacy International and two individuals. Apple has not publicly commented on the ruling.

item.title: Valve Says Rising Memory Costs Leave Steam Machine Prices Uncertain and Closes the 2TB Waitlist (2026)
item.description:
Valve says the Steam Machine could get more expensive. In an update on its hardware blog, the company said rising memory and storage costs mean it does not yet know the number of units it can build or what it will charge for them.

"We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels; as a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them," Valve wrote.

Steam Machine Stock: 512GB vs 2TB

There is good news for buyers of the cheaper model. Valve has fulfilled every reservation for the 512GB Steam Machine, and there is stock left over, so anyone can now buy one without a reservation or a waitlist. The 2TB model is a different story:

  • Valve has sent purchase invitations to every 2TB reservation holder
  • the 2TB waitlist is longer than current production and is closed to new signups
  • people already on the waitlist keep their place but have no guarantee of a machine
  • Valve says it will build fewer 2TB units than planned, even once it gets more parts

People on the 2TB waitlist can buy the 512GB model instead, but they lose their place in line if they do. When the 512GB model sells out, Valve will mark it as out of stock without opening a new waitlist. The company expects to share more about 2TB supply in January.

Why Steam Machine Prices May Rise

The Steam Machine launched about five months ago at $1,049 for the 512GB model and $1,349 for the 2TB model, both without a controller. Apart from storage, the two models are identical, with a six core Zen 4 processor, RDNA 3 graphics with 8GB of video memory and 16GB of system memory.

Those prices were based on what Valve paid for components in the six months before launch, and the company has said it already sells the Steam Machine at cost. That leaves little room to absorb further increases in RAM and SSD prices, which have climbed as demand from AI data centers grows.

Valve has raised hardware prices before. In June, it pointed to the Steam Deck OLED price increases, $240 for the 512GB model and $300 for the 1TB model, as a rough guide to how far the Steam Machine's price had already climbed from its original target.

Demand for the Steam Machine was high enough that Valve used a randomized lottery to hand out reservations. Valve has not said whether a price increase would apply to the 512GB model, the 2TB model or both.
